EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:43:58 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 EU let member states rewrite targets after they had sought recovery-fund payment, auditors find  https://euobserver.com/241815/eu-let-member-states-rewrite-targets-after-they-had-sought-recovery-fund-payment-auditors-find/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:43:58 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241815 The revised targets were "aligned with actual achieved outputs, which made the payment possible," the auditors wrote in their annual report on last year's budget. ]]> EU governments were allowed to water down targets in their post-Covid pandemic recovery plans after they had already asked Brussels for the money, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) said on Thursday (8 October).

Of 20 milestones and targets the auditors examined, 13 were amended after the member state had already submitted its payment request. In nine of those cases, the change itself was requested after the payment application had already been made. 

The revised targets were “aligned with actual achieved outputs, which made the payment possible,” the auditors wrote in their annual report on the 2025 EU budget.

Rewriting measures

Ireland, for example, asked for a payment in December 2024. But in January 2025 it requested to cut the target for ICT graduates down from 12,450 to 10,900, citing a high administrative burden.

]]> EU trade chief Šefčovič has no cards to play on China ‘ultimatum’ trip https://euobserver.com/241842/eu-trade-chief-sefcovic-faces-the-reality-of-brussels-weak-trade-hand/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:32:32 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241842 Tough rhetoric aside, the EU cannot threaten China with much if it wants to avoid a tit-for-tat trade war. But a unified position would help.]]> Persuading China that its €1bn daily trade surplus with the EU is not sustainable was always going to be a hard sell for EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič.  

And the early signs are that Šefčovič’s two days of talks with Chinese commerce secretary Wang Wentao, which conclude on Friday (9 October), are not going to deliver the breakthrough demanded by EU leaders when they gather for a summit in Brussels next week. 

“The message around the table was clear: the need to improve access to the Chinese market, while boosting our economic security,” Šefčovič posted on X ahead of the first day of talks. 

But rhetoric aside, three months after the EU Commission set up a series of ‘work streams’ with Chinese officials, with a mandate to address the multi-layered EU-Sino trade dispute, it is hard to see much tangible progress. 

Hours before Šefčovič arrived, Beijing rejected an EU demand for so-called “voluntary export restrictions” on its electric vehicles (EVs). 

In August, data published by Schmidt Automotive Research found that 14 percent of EV sales across Europe this year were Chinese-made, up from 9.4 percent last year. 

That is despite the EU imposing additional tariffs of between 17 and 36 percent on Chinese EVs in October 2024.

]]> EU pleads with Russian authorities to lift the lid on plague death in Siberia https://euobserver.com/241721/eu-pleads-with-russian-authorities-to-lift-the-lid-on-plague-death-in-siberia/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:08:16 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241721 The European Commission has joined the WHO and US in calling on Russia to share information on the sudden death of a lab technician in a bio-research facility. But the Kremlin has said there is nothing to see.]]> First published in Respekt, adapted by EUobserver

Unsavoury news comes from Russia country often these days. But the latest unexpected development is the spread of a deadly disease.

Behind the mysterious death of a young woman in Siberia in early October was reportedly pneumonic plague – a disease so contagious it is considered as bad as anthrax, smallpox, and Ebola.

Local authorities in Russia have denied the plague as cause of death, but despite this, they have implemented anti-epidemic measures.

Eva Hrncirova, a spokesperson for the European Commission, said on Thursday (8 October): “Russia should make information about the plague available as soon as possible. This is what we need”.

“We had a meeting with the member states yesterday within the [EU Commission’s] Health Security Committee, and with the WHO [World Health Organization], who are in contact with our delegation in Moscow,” she said.

Russia was asked by the WHO to share “timely, precise, and exact information” about the possible plague in Siberia, she also said.

“We don’t have enough information to assess the epidemiological situation,” she added.

Nothing to see here, says Russia

Pneumonic plague disease can be treated with antibiotics if detected early, but officials beyond Russia’s borders are left with worrying questions.

Did an Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute lab technician in Shelekhov (Siberia) really die of plague?

If so, was it a natural version of the disease, or a more dangerous bacterium modified in military labs?

And what is the risk of the Middle Ages-era disease spreading?

Pneumonic plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis — the same one that once brought devastating plague epidemics known as the Black Death.

The pneumonic form of plague, a disease that killed up to half of Europe’s population in the 14th century, spreads through droplets by coughing or sneezing.

It manifests as severe, rapidly developing pneumonia that almost always ends in death if left untreated. But if antibiotics are administered in time (ideally within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms), the disease is treatable.

Independent Russian-language media say that Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory technician at the research and hygiene institute in question, accidentally broke a test tube containing plague bacteria in late September, became infected and died in hospital several days later, on 2 October.

Authorities have not confirmed the cause of the woman’s death, letting on only that she died of pneumonia and claiming that no microorganisms connected with her work had been found in her body.

Some 200 of her contacts were subsequently put into quarantine with medical supervision.

Authorities also ordered a three-week quarantine at several hospitals in the wider area, and facemasks for the wider population – even for schoolchildren.

Read more

EU has ‘learned nothing’ from Covid say MEPs, as mpox outbreak grows

Russia’s neighbours, Mongolia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, have all introduced border controls.

Russia said the epidemic situation in the area was stable, that none of the deceased woman’s contacts had shown signs of infection, and that there was no cause for concern.

However, the head of Russia’s public health authority reportedly travelled to Irkutsk to attend a meeting with local officials, while residents of Shelekhov report that people in protective suits are moving around the town.

And epidemiologists say it is simply not possible that Russia’s public health service would resort to such dramatic measures, including closing hospitals, over a single case of ‘pneumonia of unknown origin’ .

The institute where the laboratory technician worked is said to be a civilian facility that, among other things, researches and monitors the incidence of plague.

In Siberia, especially near the borders with China and Mongolia, the bacteria in question still circulate among animals and occasionally infect humans, as they do in some parts of Africa, where the disease is most common.

]]> Trapped under Russian occupation, people in Oleshky forced to eat dogs to survive (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,687) https://euobserver.com/241776/trapped-under-russian-occupation-people-in-oleshky-forced-to-eat-dogs-to-survive-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1687/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:01:19 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241776 Witnesses describe an occupied town where a hospital director feeds only pro-Russian loyalists, others boil weeds or eat dogs to survive, and Russian troops punish anyone caught accepting Ukrainian aid dropped in by drone.]]>
  • Horrifying stories from the occupied Ukrainian town are mounting.
  • Two clans have emerged in Oleshky — those who support Putin can get food.
  • According to experts, Russia is fundamentally violating international law and using residents’ vulnerability as a weapon.
  • Putin’s tragic gift: the death toll in Pryluky rose to 22; 12 people were killed on a bus the following day.
  • Maps of the day: Operation Vivaldi continues to make gains in Donbas.
  • Videos of the day: an FPV drone attacked a fully occupied quad bike; a refinery is on fire.

    • Horrifying stories from the occupied town are mounting. The situation in Russian-occupied Oleshky, in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, has long been extremely tense.

    Around 2,000 residents have long faced a severe humanitarian crisis and isolation. Before the Russian invasion, 24,000 people lived in the town.

    And the situation of local residents left behind shows how Russia, as an occupying power, treats civilians brutally and deliberately violates international agreements.

    “There is a lack of food and healthcare. Since the destruction of the hydroelectric power plant, there has been no drinking water, electricity or gas. They do not even have wood for heating. Not only is it impossible to live with dignity, it is also impossible to bury people with dignity, because the occupiers even prohibit the burial of the dead,” Tetiana Hasanenko, head of Ukraine’s military administration for Oleshky, told Denník N.

    Russia is also using Oleshky to shell the right bank of the Dnipro, especially the city of Kherson, just nine km away. Fierce fighting is under way over the surrounding islets. This turns Oleshky residents into human shields and prevents their safe evacuation.

    According to the BBC, Oleshky is trapped by both geography and war. “To the north and west, it is cut off by the river and destroyed bridges, while to the south and east it is cut off by dangerous or impassable roads,” the report said.

    The situation in the town had already been dramatic in 2023, when the destruction of the Kakhovka dam caused flooding.

    A few days ago, special units of the SBU security service and Ukraine’s National Guard launched, according to the RBK-Ukraine website, a new operation to deliver humanitarian packages containing food, water and medicines across the Dnipro.

    The aid totalled around four tonnes, with each package weighing 19 kg.

    Footage from the mission can be viewed in this video by Suspilne television.

    In these difficult conditions, heavy Vampire drones — dubbed Baba Yaga by Russians — are, according to a Ukrainian website, one of the few ways of providing aid to people on the occupied side of the river. Ukrainian soldiers often deploy them at the front for their own logistics in areas that are extremely dangerous.

    Last year, the drone was even described as the most effective combat vehicle changing the course of the war.

    According to Hasanenko, Ukraine’s armed forces have regularly dropped food by drone into the occupied area since March.

    “They did it, but not on such a large scale. And every time drones fly over, the occupiers punish local people for it,” said the Ukrainian woman, who is in contact with people from Oleshky.

    She said people try to immediately transfer the aid into unmarked containers to avoid punishment. “The occupiers believe that if people accept help from the Ukrainian armed forces, they supposedly have some connection with them and are betraying the country — which is not actually their country. And that is why they punish them,” Hasanenko explained.

    In recent months, Oleshky residents have relied mainly on their own harvests, but at the end of the season they face a critical food shortage.

    There have even been reports that residents were forced to eat dogs. A BBC report from late September revealed shocking findings from the town: people had learned to cook even with weeds.

    Some, according to Ukrainska Pravda, caught pigeons or pheasants, while others cooked borscht “in a new way” — from eggs, courgettes, tomatoes and herbs.

    “Prices there are not merely high but almost astronomical. Eggs sell for 800 hryvnias a dozen (€19), potatoes and onions for 500 (€11.90), courgettes for 250 (€5.95), and tomatoes for 200 (€4.76), because there was a good harvest,” the website wrote.

    Despite the risk of being killed by a mine, residents travel along a “road of death”, lined with burnt-out cars, to the nearest town, Radensk, for food. This was also confirmed by Reuters, which spoke to people who still have relatives there.

    “The choice Russia imposes on civilians every day: stay and die of hunger, or leave and risk being blown up by a landmine,” the agency quoted Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets as saying.

    Two categories of people and harassment over humanitarian aid. In the hospital, where dead bodies have been lying in the basement for four months, people have been divided into two clans, according to witnesses.

    “Those loyal to the Russian regime have some food, sometimes even meat and alcohol. The people they call Ukraine-lovers have nothing. The hospital director took everything from the latest deliveries provided as humanitarian aid and handed it out to his own people,” Ukrainska Pravda quoted the son of a man who remained in Oleshky as saying.

    When Ukrainians succeeded in dropping humanitarian aid into Oleshky, a new phase of psychological warfare by the Russian Federation began.

    Under normal circumstances, an operation to drop humanitarian aid would not attract so much attention, but according to Ukraine’s SBU security service, the Russian response reached particularly absurd proportions.

    According to its information, Russian soldiers were ordered to arrange a series of interviews aimed at discrediting the Ukrainian side.

    The recorded interviews were meant to include claims that Ukrainians were shelling Oleshky, positive views of Putin’s regime and expressions of gratitude. The SBU therefore urged Ukrainians to treat such reports cautiously and not spread unverified information.

    According to information from the Ukrainian resistance movement in the Kherson region, which cannot be independently verified, those who received the aid faced abuse during interrogations.

    According to Hasanenko, the most important thing now is to evacuate people from the town.

    “Even what humanitarian missions are doing now, dropping food, will not solve their problems. I have reports in which people wrote that they had food left for two days and that this saved them. But it will not save them forever. Many people are dying there because of drones and artillery shelling. We need to establish a humanitarian corridor,” said the head of Oleshky’s military administration, adding that last winter had already been difficult and that they might not survive this one.

    She herself has received reports that people have lost 10, 20 or even 40 kg. “There is one case: a woman wrote that she weighed 110 kg and now weighs 67. She has lost 40 kg and writes to me that she is dying.”

    Violations of international law. During the recent UN General Assembly session, Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha spoke about Oleshky. Ukraine’s main aim, he said, was to establish a humanitarian corridor in the area and safely evacuate people who have not accepted the Russian occupation.

    It is precisely because of this stance, Kyiv says, that the Russian army is retaliating by blockading the town, where tourists had before the war come for its unique natural environment of pine forests and Dnipro inlets.

    “There is no supply of electricity or gas. Over the past month, the delivery of food, medicines and other basic necessities has been completely blocked. Horrifying testimonies are coming from occupied Oleshky about how people are trying to survive under a blockade imposed by Russia: they are looking for scraps of food and gathering grass because there is simply no other food,” Ukrainian website NV quoted the foreign minister as saying.

    Another dimension of Russian terror, he said, is the hunting of civilians. Russian FPV drones pursue and attack people, turning even an attempt to leave one’s home or move around the town into a deadly risk.

    According to TSN, Russia is artificially creating food shortages in Oleshky, selling an ordinary food package for 50,000 hryvnias — nearly €1,000 — compared with a standard price of up to 2,000 hryvnias (€40). When people have no money, they offer their jewellery in exchange for food.

    Food was last delivered to the town at the end of May, and according to Ukrainska Pravda, no further attempt to bring in food was made. When locals tried on 2 June, their four cars were blown up by anti-personnel mines, killing two people.

    Legally, the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, as well as the use of the population as human shields, constitutes, according to Ukrainian website Rubryka, a violation of the Fourth Geneva Convention — on the protection of civilians in time of war — and a war crime under Article 8 of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC).

    An occupying power is responsible for those living in occupied territory. “It must provide people with food, medical care and proper sanitation. But Russia is indifferent to all international requirements,” Ukrainska Pravda wrote.

    According to the Institute for the Study of War, Oleshky has become a test of Russian dominance in an area “characterised by population decline, damaged infrastructure, chronic insecurity and growing isolation from the rest of Ukraine”.

    Rather than reversing these conditions, the think tank said, Russia governs through them.

    “Oleshky demonstrates that the humanitarian crisis unfolding across many Russian-occupied communities is not merely a byproduct of war but increasingly appears to be the result of an occupation system that tolerates, exploits, and sustains civilian vulnerability as a means of maintaining control,” wrote US experts.

    According to Hasanenko, Russian fears of Ukrainian operations are also behind this. “I think they are simply trying to prevent the Ukrainian armed forces from crossing the Dnipro, because they could begin liberating the left bank. And people simply serve as human shields for them, while they mine everything completely,” she told EUobserver.

    A tragic toll on Putin’s birthday. At least 22 people were killed, including five children, in a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile attack on an apartment building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region, on 7 October. Rescue workers pulled many people from the rubble of the destroyed building. According to local authorities, Russia fired as many as six cruise missiles at the town.

    “This is the ‘gift’ Putin gave himself for his birthday. Killing children, killing people. There were new attacks with Shahed drones and aerial bombs during the day. It is important that leaders do not remain silent about what happened,” said Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky, calling on the West to help with air defence.

    Brutal Russian attacks continued the following day. As many as 12 people were killed after Russia hit a bus in the Donbas city of Kramatorsk. Putin’s regime is currently facing a crisis at the front, which it is trying to address through massive shelling of Ukrainian cities.

    Maps of the day

    Ukraine’s successful Operation Vivaldi continues. According to a report by the Institute for the Study of War, Ukrainian forces are continuing counterattacks towards the eastern bank of the Zherebets River, northeast of Lyman. The numerical superiority of Ukrainian forces and drones there is preventing Russian forces from consolidating their positions in the town.

    According to September statistics, which we wrote about a few days ago, Russia has just had its worst month in Donbas for the past three years. The US newspaper The New York Times also charted this on its map.

    Videos of the day

    Smoke over a distant refinery. Ukraine continues to launch drone attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Most recently, it caused a fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat plant in the Bashkir region, one of Russia’s largest refineries. It is located around 1,300 km from the front line.

    A fatal quad bike ride. The Hornets of Dovbush, from the 68th Brigade, released a video showing five Russian soldiers on a quad bike coming into view of their FPV attack drone. The location of the attack is unknown.

    What are the losses

    No update on Thursday.

    • By Monday (5 October), Russia had verifiably lost 24,170 pieces of heavy equipment (24,138 on Tuesday, 22 September). Of these, Ukrainians destroyed 19,133 (19,105), 1,003 (1,000) were damaged, 1,194 (1,194) were abandoned by their crews, and the Ukrainian army captured 2,840 (2,839). This includes 4,452 (4,448) tanks, of which 3,357 (3,353) were destroyed in combat.
    • Ukraine lost 12,238 (12,175) pieces of equipment, of which 9,633 (9,579) were destroyed, 711 (702) were damaged, 695 (695) were abandoned and 1,199 (1,199) were captured. This includes 1,466 (1,464) tanks, of which 1,126 (1,125) were destroyed in combat.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its own dead or destroyed equipment. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. This overview uses data from the Oryx project, which has compiled a list of equipment losses documented exclusively by photographs since the start of the war.

    ]]>         EU agency Frontex told Libyans where to find migrant boat with children, then watched them run it over https://euobserver.com/241745/eu-agency-frontex-told-libyans-where-to-find-migrant-boat-with-children-then-watched-them-run-it-over/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 13:27:10 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241745 The 19 June incident saw the Libyans once again attacking people fleeing the country on boats after having first been informed of their location by Frontex, an EU agency based in Warsaw.]]> The EU’s border agency, Frontex, shared coordinates of an overcrowded and partly deflated boat in the Mediterranean sea with the Libyan coastguard and then watched them run it over.

    The boat was carrying 27 people, including children.

    The findings, by Frontex’s own fundamental rights officer, described an incident that took place on 19 June 2026.

    And this was just a tiny part of a wider pattern of violence by the EU-backed Libyan coastguard, which has also shot at or near civil rescue vessels.

    No one was killed in the June event. But people were tossed into the water. Others, pulled onto the Libyan vessel, were then beaten by Libyan uniformed officers.

    Frontex had issued a Mayday relay and then shared the sightings by email with the Libyan rescue centre.

    No vessels were reported to be in the vicinity, but the Libyans showed up 90 minutes later.

    The internal Frontex findings highlight ongoing tensions in the agency over sharing rescue coordinates with the Libyans in the name of saving lives.

    “Saving lives is the absolute sort of absolute right that people have,” Hans Leijtens the agency’s director, told EUobserver earlier this year.

    “And it’s our job to contribute to that, and if that sort of starts with looking at which part of the Mediterranean ship is sailing, and if it’s a north African country, we all have to inform the authorities there,” he added.

    But his own rights officer also notes that the botched rescue on 19 June amounted to a violation of the right to life, citing article six of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

    He says the standard is not simply whether the migrants were ultimately rescued, but if the operation was planned and executed to minimise risks to human life.

    In this case, the Libyans violated that right among others, he says. Frontex did not reply to the findings in the report, as of publication.

    Let the court decide

    ]]>         French school protests to continue, after prime minister ignores demands https://euobserver.com/241687/french-school-protests-to-continue-after-prime-minister-ignores-demands/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:21:56 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241687 Two-weeks long protests by French high-school students demanding better education conditions risk getting more heated due the French government's lack of response.]]> Two-weeks long protests by French high-school students demanding better education conditions risk getting more heated due to the French government’s lack of response.

    For his part, French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu told parliament on Wednesday (7 October) the first proposals on education reform would be published at the end of the month.

    He spoke after 250,000 demonstrators took to the streets across the country on Tuesday (6 October), according to interior ministry fiigures.

    But the High School Student Union (Union Syndicaire Lycéenne, USL) said the number was as high as 450,000, including solidarity protests in most universities.

    ]]>         Morocco’s surveillance state does not stop at Western Sahara — and Europe can no longer pretend not to know https://euobserver.com/241454/moroccos-surveillance-state-does-not-stop-at-western-sahara-and-europe-can-no-longer-pretend-not-to-know/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:50:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241454 As new evidence emerges of Moroccan spying on Sahrawi activists, including in Europe, European governments continue to deepen their security ties with Rabat without seriously questioning how those capabilities are being used.]]> In April 2021, I told The Guardian that Sahrawi activists were having their phones and internet connections hacked.

    Our position is clear: large global companies that benefit most from Europe’s single market should contribute fairly to the EU budget that makes those benefits possible.

    Cutting the EU budget may look like saving money. But if it means weaker competitiveness, less social investment and a less secure Europe, we save nothing and taxpayers foot the bill.

    Unlike his predecessor, Oleksandr Syrskyi, Drapatyi does not promote himself much on social media. He has not made a single Facebook post since July, and his Telegram profile has similarly remained silent.

    Ukrainska Pravda journalist Olha Kyrylenko tried to fill this “information vacuum”. She spoke with around 20 senior officers in the Ukrainian army.

    Based on their anonymous testimonies, she sought to convey how Drapatyi had changed the Ukrainian army over those two and a half months.

    The army is currently performing well at the front: Russians are suffering heavy losses and advancing very slowly, if at all. The protection of military, industrial and civilian sites in the rear against Russian air attacks is worse.

    Drapatyi gives units considerable freedom and does not seek to micromanage everything at the front, as Syrskyi did.

    “Unlike his predecessor, who told some brigade commanders how and where they should fight — and even specified the coordinates where they should establish a position — Drapatyi chose a different approach. He decided to decentralise command and abandon ‘micromanagement’,” Kyrylenko wrote.

    The newspaper also adds that Drapatyi travels to visit units less frequently.

    After taking up the post of commander-in-chief, he made several personnel changes. Broadly speaking, he is promoting younger commanders proven in the current war to replace older officers of the old Soviet school.

    By contrast, he is moving the latter to rear-area and training roles, or they are retiring.

    They are being replaced by younger commanders; Drapatyi himself is only 43. For example, Denys Prokopenko, a general with a far-right past, was put in charge of the important area near Dobropillia, where Russians are currently exerting the greatest pressure, despite being only 35.

    ]]>         Sanctions in February, handshakes in September: EU’s flip-flop Iran policy is putting lives at risk https://euobserver.com/241462/sanctions-in-february-handshakes-in-september-eus-flip-flop-iran-policy-is-putting-lives-at-risk/ Wed, 07 Oct 2026 10:42:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241462 By sitting down with senior Iranian figures who publicly back the Revolutionary Guard while keeping sanctions limited to technocratic lists, EU governments risk undermining their own leverage at a time of rising regional tensions.]]> Why would the European Union list the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organisation in February, and then, seven months later, have its top diplomat sit down with the foreign minister of the government the Guard Corps defends?

    At the UN General Assembly last month, EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas met Abbas Araghchi, who served in the Guard Corps during the Iran–Iraq war.

    Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten met president Masoud Pezeshkian, who in 2019 joined fellow parliamentarians in wearing the Guard Corps uniform to protest Washington’s terrorist designation of it. France, Italy, and Norway held meetings of their own.

    These talks came less than nine months after Iranian security forces, on 8 and 9 January, killed protesters on a scale without precedent in the country’s modern history.

    The human rights group HRANA has verified more than 7,000 deaths, and the UN special rapporteur warned that the toll may exceed 20,000.

    In September, the UN fact-finding mission concluded that the crackdown amounted to crimes against humanity. Nor has the killing stopped: Iran Human Rights counted at least 532 executions in the first eight months of this year, including protesters arrested in January.

    After a massacre, a foreign policy guided by European values should pursue one aim above others: making a repetition more costly for those who would order and carry it out.

    Naming and shaming raises the reputational cost of repression, targeted sanctions raise its material cost, and delegitimisation raises the political cost of staying loyal to the regime.

    They work only in combination, since sanctions without delegitimization tell the regime’s elite that their assets are at risk, but their standing is not.

    Read more

    Why the Iran uprising is Europe’s strategic blind spot

    EU vs US sanctions

    Europe has used the first two instruments. The EU listed the Guard Corps in February and sanctioned additional Iranian officials for human rights abuses.

    However, these measures target assets and individuals, while the government that presided over the killing keeps its seat at the top table.

    The UNGA in New York showed how little the third instrument has been used.

    The terrorist listing freezes the Guard Corps’ funds. Neither Araghchi nor Pezeshkian is on an EU sanctions list.

    Yet it leaves a question unanswered: how far should the logic of a terrorist designation extend to the government that funds and publicly defends it?

    Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union requires the Union’s external action to be guided by human rights and to be consistent.

    Branding the Guard Corps a terrorist organisation in Brussels while posing for photographs with the government it defends in New York sits uneasily with that obligation.

    This inconsistency is costly. In a study in foreign policy analysis, my co-authors and I examined how Iranians reacted to US sanctions. Comprehensive sanctions produced a rally around the government, even among reformists.

    The 2019 designation of the Guard Corps, by contrast, produced almost no rally outside the regime’s hardliner core. Thus, targeted pressure on the security apparatus does not drive Iranians into its arms.

    Handshakes, on the other hand, may give the apparatus exactly what targeted sanctions are meant to withhold: international legitimacy.

    The photographs from New York reach two audiences.

    The first sits inside the state: an officer deciding whether to fire on a crowd, or to step aside, weighs one question above most others, namely whether the regime will survive, and each of those photographs suggests an answer.

    The second audience is the families of those killed, executed, and blinded since January. For them, the message is that Europe has moved on after eight months.

    Read more

    Reporting when the internet goes dark

    A picture is worth a thousand words

    I am not against diplomacy. Kallas raised the sharp rise in executions with Araghchi, and Jetten raised human rights and Iranian actions on Dutch soil with Pezeshkian. Channels on shipping, detained Europeans, and de-escalation should stay open.

    My objection concerns the level and the format: a meeting between leaders, photographed at the General Assembly with no public conditions attached, is not a technical channel.

    Concerns voiced in private do not travel as far as the photograph, which signals normal relations with a government that has done nothing to earn them.

    Four steps would help.

    First, the Council should agree on a common line: contact at the technical and envoy level, and leader-level meetings only on public conditions, beginning with a halt to protest-related executions.

    Second, human rights sanctions should move up the chain of command, to those who answer politically for the security forces.

    Third, member states should invest in accountability that does not depend on Tehran, such as universal jurisdiction cases and evidence-sharing with the UN mission.

    Finally, Europe should engage openly with Iran’s democratic opposition.

    The EU has already decided, in law, what the Guard Corps is. Its leaders have yet to act accordingly. A massacre answered with sanctions in February and handshakes in September does not raise the cost of the next one. It lowers it.

Nowhere is that question more urgent than in Europe, which funds the world's most comprehensive welfare states primarily through taxes on work.]]> Every major technological shift reshapes not just the economy but the tax system that pays for it. When big corporations emerged, corporate and payroll taxes followed. When mass car ownership took hold, fuel duties emerged to pay for the roads it required. 

    As AI shifts work from people to machines, it will force a rethink of who gets taxed, on what, and where. Nowhere is that question more urgent than in Europe, which funds the world’s most comprehensive welfare states primarily through taxes on work.

    Taxes on work make up 51.5 percent of all tax revenue in the EU-27, according to the European Commission’s latest Taxation Trends data — a share that rose in 2024. These charges are taken straight from the payslip. They’re hard to avoid, and scale with employment.

    AI, by replacing human work with software and machines, eats away at exactly this tax base. 

    The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates that around 40 percent of jobs worldwide are exposed to AI. If that leads to fewer workers, it will also mean fewer payslips, pension contributions and social charges, weakening the revenue streams that fund Europe’s pension and healthcare systems. This is not a distant problem; the costs are already mounting.

    Read more

    EU not ‘lagging’ US in AI-productivity gains, Lagarde tells MEPs

    Shift the burden to corporate profits

    The obvious response is to shift more of the tax burden onto corporate profits, which will increasingly reflect the gains firms make by deploying AI instead of hiring workers.

    Unlike a tax on machines and equipment themselves, a profit tax falls mostly on excess profits and need not distort investment. The case for shifting weight from payroll taxes to profits is strong and strengthens as AI replaces more workers with machines.

    But profits, unlike payrolls, move. A company can locate its intellectual property in a low-rate jurisdiction — a pattern Europe knows well from decades of profits routed through Ireland and Luxembourg — and ensure that profits are booked far from where the jobs are lost. It is how the world’s largest technology and AI firms already operate.

    Read more

    Reverse centaurs: EU approach to AI risks dystopia for human workers

    Two-pillar answer

    The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD’s) Inclusive Framework was designed to address exactly this: profits shifted across jurisdictions to avoid tax, and e-commerce allowed sales where firms have no physical presence. AI makes these reforms more urgent. 

    Pillar One of the framework put forward by the Paris-based wealthy nations’ club addresses where a corporation is taxed. It shifts partial taxing rights for the largest multinationals away from where they are headquartered and toward where their customers and users are located. 

    Still under negotiation, it would apply only to a handful of the largest firms, but many AI companies would qualify. 

    These firms are concentrated in a select number of countries, very few of them European, but the displacement they cause, and the public services that displaced workers will require, will weigh heavily on European budgets.

    Pillar Two of the OECD framework introduces a global minimum corporate tax of 15 percent on multinationals with revenues above €750m.

    The EU moved first and furthest: Council Directive (EU) 2022/2523 made the minimum tax binding across the Union from 2024, and 22 of the 27 member states now apply it in full. The United States, notably, has not implemented the rules. 

    Read more

    Let’s not allow AI firms to use fears of future dystopias to distract Europeans from existing problems

    Politics is undermining the fix

    But the obstacles are real. US ratification of the OECD proposals is unlikely, and many of the largest companies are headquartered there. 

    The pressure is already reshaping Europe’s own rules: under the G7’s June 2025 ‘side-by-side’ agreement, US-parented groups would be exempt from the EU’s minimum-tax rules: a carveout the European Commission confirmed in January 2026 and which several member states consider legally fragile. 

    The Commission also dropped its proposed EU digital levy under US trade pressure, leaving a patchwork of national digital services taxes in France, Italy, Spain, Austria, and elsewhere.

    Such exceptions and carveouts show that big-power politics can hollow out the framework. These reforms were designed to address the tax challenges for an AI-economy. They were good policy then. They are fiscal necessities now. Fairer corporate taxation will not be enough, but it is a start. 

    Europe’s choice

    The EU has instruments on the table, the BEFIT common corporate tax base and the proposed Corporate Resource for Europe, but both remain politically contested.

    European governments that fail to act will be managing the social costs of technological disruption with a tax system built for the industrial age, while the profits that fund their rivals accumulate beyond their reach.

    Even if Europeans work less, their needs for health care, pensions, and consumption remain. As wage-based contributions shrink, Europe must shift more of the tax burden onto corporate profits and close off the routes that let those profits move beyond the reach of the states bearing the costs of automation. 

    Productivity gains may soften the arithmetic; they will not repeal it. The tax base must follow the economy.

    Read more

    THIS WEEK: EU trade chief heads to China as Brussels unveils long-delayed pre-enlargement reforms

    That’s the case with Stellantis and Chinese manufacturer Leapmotor. And now Dongfeng is also negotiating to produce cars at the French plant of Rennes La Janais. Because by moving production to Europe, Chinese manufacturers may be losing one of their main advantages, which is cheap labour.

    But low labour costs are only one part of their competitive edge.

    Chinese manufacturers also continue to benefit from state support. And setting up production in Europe doesn’t necessarily mean building brand-new factories.

    In many cases, Chinese companies are looking to partner with European manufacturers and use factories that are already there — factories that are no longer operating at full capacity. That means they can save significantly on investment costs. And they can also rely on their European partners’ existing sales and distribution networks.

    So how big is this Chinese presence in Europe becoming? For 2028, there are already 12 projects involving Chinese carmakers setting up production in Europe. Several are in Spain, with others in France, Belgium, Slovakia, Hungary, Sweden and Austria.

    Read more

    [Interview] EU’s carmakers face their own Nokia challenge to survive Chinese threat, says industry expert

    Now, why would European manufacturers allow their Chinese competitors to produce cars in their own factories? Part of the answer is that European carmakers are struggling to keep up in electric vehicles sells. And that is contributing to factory closures and job losses.

    European manufacturers have to meet EU targets on average CO2 emissions each year. And producing more electric vehicles is necessary to meet those requirements.

    So partnerships with Chinese manufacturers can serve two purposes: they can help European companies fulfilling their green cars objectives, while also keeping existing factories and jobs running.

    Though there is a longer-term risk for European manufacturers. The more Chinese companies establish themselves in Europe, the more competitive pressure they could put on European brands — potentially even leading to takeovers. That has happened before: Volvo Cars, for example, was acquired by Chinese group Geely in 2010. 

    In Germany, carmakers are for now refusing to open the doors of their production sites to the Chinese. But they do have partnerships with Chinese companies to produce vehicles in China, where they can benefit from lower production costs. That explains why they were very much opposed to imposing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.

    Read more

    Volkswagen benefited from €1.5bn in German EV subsidies as it lobbies EU to hit Chinese cars harder

    But the situation is now changing. Volkswagen closed its Dresden factory last year, and other German plants are also facing closure risks. Germany’s car industry is therefore increasingly joining calls for stronger protection against Chinese competition.

    And that brings us back to the Franco-German paper that is circulating in Brussels, which calls for measures to restrict Chinese access to the European market.

    Because this debate goes well beyond cars. The EU is increasingly concerned about Chinese competition and dependence in a range of strategic industries. This will be discussed next week, when EU leaders meet in Brussels.

    The European Commission could also present a new so-called “diversification” tool, either at the summit or around it. One possibility would be to require companies not to rely exclusively on China for certain critical materials. Something which could trigger what we call a trade war. I’ll be following that very closely!

    ]]>

      <description><p>Suit says AI tool allows independently owned franchises to exchange nonpublic price and sales information</p><p>McDonald’s is facing a lawsuit in federal court over its alleged use of an <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">AI</a> tool to determine pricing across independent franchises, which prosecutors say violates antitrust laws and has unfairly inflated menu prices for Americans.</p><p>The vast majority of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/mcdonalds">McDonald’s</a> US stores are independently owned and are said to individually decide on prices under company policy.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/06/ai-misuse-brand-reputation</link>
      <description><p>The findings come after warnings from tech leaders that AI placed in the wrong hands could trigger larger threats such as nuclear war or bioweaponry destruction</p><p>Misusing <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">artificial intelligence</a> (AI) is the top threat to companies’ reputations – more so than being accused of putting children in the way of mental, emotional or physical harm and issues exposed by the US-Israel war on Iran, among other brand risks, according to a new survey of more than 150 public affairs leaders.</p><p>Those findings in the new edition of the quarterly Reputation Risk Index, released on Tuesday, came on the heels of other perhaps more dire warnings from leading tech figures that AI in the wrong hands could <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/commentisfree/2026/sep/23/how-would-ai-actually-kill-all-humans-here-are-the-top-five-most-likely-scenarios">precipitate</a> existential threats on a mass scale such as nuclear war or destruction by bioweaponry.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/06/ai-misuse-brand-reputation">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Millionaire tax no more? Rightwing groups lead effort to repeal Washington state law</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax</link>
      <description><p>An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the 9.9% tax on earnings above $1m – who’s winning the fight? </p><p>Voters in Washington state will soon decide the fate of the state’s so-called “<a href="https://senatedemocrats.wa.gov/millionaires-tax-faq/">millionaire tax</a>” – a 9.9% income tax on earnings above $1m that was <a href="https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-signs-millionaires-tax-law">signed</a> into law in March and is now facing a conservative-backed effort to repeal it.</p><p>An <a href="https://leg.wa.gov/media/ucubvqsd/2026-summary-of-initiative-26-645.pdf">initiative</a> on November’s ballot aims to overturn the tax, claiming that the tax represents a slippery slope, and would eventually result in taxes for more than just millionaires. A <a href="https://no645.com/our-coalition/">coalition</a> of advocacy groups and unions opposing the initiative say taxing the state’s 20,000 highest-earning households could raise approximately $3.5bn in necessary annual revenue to fund core priorities like education and healthcare, and expand tax credits and sales tax exemptions.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 08 Oct 2026 17:29:24 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Elon Musk’s ‘X’ loses High Court challenge handling of complaints]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/08/elon-musks-x-loses-high-court-challenge-handling-of-complaints/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/08/elon-musks-x-loses-high-court-challenge-handling-of-complaints/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 17:26:23 +0000Elon Musk’s X, formerly known as Twitter, has failed in a High Court bid challenging how the Irish media regulator, Comisiún na Meán, deals with user complaints against social media platforms.

On Thursday, Judge Cian Ferriter ruled that the commission is entitled under law to refer information from complaints made under the Digital Services Act to a “supervisory” unit, which also has the power to retain those complaints to identify possible future compliance issues.

X had submitted that the commission could not legally refer information garnered from complaints to the supervision team if those complaints were already concluded or undetermined. They also submitted that information contained within those complaints could not be used for broader, future systemic investigations and that the regulator had therefore acted outside of the law.

X further submitted that it regularly takes “unilateral” removal action, such as in cases of child exploitation, which it is obligated to do by its own regulatory policies. The company submitted that the commission was acting in an “extra statutory” manner.

X had argued that complainants were entitled to an outcome instead of the commission “kicking the can down the road without notification” on any possible future purported breaches.

David Fennelly, senior counsel for the regulator, had said that X was attempting to undermine the watchdog’s important role in cases that had implications across the EU.

The judge said in his judgment that the commission has discretion as to who investigates complaints, adding: “In the circumstances, I do not believe it can be said that the commission improperly disabled itself from exercising its statutory discretion by reference to any of the matters available to it.”

The judge said there was no “improper fettering of discretion involved and no legally impermissible steps on the part of the Commission or its delegates”.

]]>Evan Vucci<![CDATA[Kingspan faces €40m fine over abandoned deal for Slovenian rival ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/kingspan-faces-40m-fine-over-abandoned-deal-for-slovenian-rival/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/kingspan-faces-40m-fine-over-abandoned-deal-for-slovenian-rival/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 17:16:54 +0000Insulation maker Kingspan faces a €40 million fine for misleading European Commission competition regulators during their investigation of its bid for Slovenian rival, Trimo.

Kingspan ultimately dropped plans to buy the roofing and insulation materials manufacturer in 2022. The planned transaction had triggered a commission investigation into the deal’s potential impact on competition in several insulation panel markets.

The Commission has now fined Kingspan €40 million for providing “incorrect and misleading information” to its review of the Irish group’s bid for Trimo in 2021, a statement said on Thursday.

The Co Cavan-based multinational said it would appeal the ruling.

Kingspan misled the commission on how it tracks the use of mineral fibre sandwich boards, the insulation product made by both companies, against other insulation materials, the statement noted.

The Irish group provided incorrect or misleading information about the availability of bidding data, generally used to assess the competitiveness of a given industry, the Commission said.

It also provided incorrect or misleading information on research and development carried out by Kingspan into mineral fibre sandwich panels.

“This kind of information, which usually only the company itself can provide, is key to understanding a company’s position in the relevant market,” said the commission.

In addition, Kingspan gave incorrect or misleading information about its board members’ involvement in the planned acquisition of Trimo, other deals considered by Kingspan and industry trends and strategy, the commission added.

Kingspan gave the incorrect or misleading information to the commission in either its notification of the proposed acquisition of Trimo or in replies to requests for information under EU merger rules, according to the statement.

The commission has fined Kingspan €10 million for each of the four breaches of merger regulations that it identified.

The EU executive body said it considered Kingspan’s infringements serious as they obstructed the mergers investigation, making it difficult for the commission to properly review the transaction.

“It also considers that Kingspan could not have been unaware of its obligations under the EU merger regulation, meaning that the breach was at least negligent,” the commission said.

“In particular, the commission found that Kingspan asserted the non-existence of key documents, misrepresented facts, or claimed the impossibility to provide key information that only Kingspan was in a position to provide,” it added.

Kingspan responded that it noted the commission’s decision regarding a deal that it ultimately decided not to pursue.

“We look forward to appealing the decision in full,” the Irish group said.

Kingspan did not comment beyond that. But when the commission first questioned the information the company provided to the mergers investigation in March 2024, the group said that it had fully co-operated with the European authorities throughout the Trimo bid.

“This Trimo application was unusual and uniquely onerous given both the level of information sought and the fact that the process occurred during Covid,” Kingspan noted at the time.

“It is in no way representative of the long and productive relationship that Kingspan has with the European Commission.”

Kingspan pointed out that, by March 2024, the Commission had approved four other acquisitions completed by the Irish group since 2020 when it first bid for Trimo.

The European Commission routinely investigates mergers across member states to assess their potential impact on goods and services.

]]><![CDATA[Home heating oil surges 58% as energy bill hikes wipe out budget gains]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/home-heating-oil-prices-rise-almost-60/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/home-heating-oil-prices-rise-almost-60/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 11:06:37 +0000Families face bills of €1,600 to heat their homes this winter as soaring energy prices threaten to wipe out workers’ budget tax gains.

Home heating oil prices rose by 58.6 per cent in September when compared with the same month last year, new figures from the Central Statistics Office (CSO) released on Thursday show.

Sharp rises in energy prices sparked by the US-Iran war helped drive up the cost of living by 4.1 per in the 12 months to September, the highest increase in two years, according to the CSO.

The cost of filling a 1,000 litre domestic oil tank now varies between €1,500 and €1,600, according to Daragh Cassidy, head of communications at price comparison website, Bonkers.ie.

“It’s gone up €250 since the start of August and €400 since June and July,” he added.

Around 700,000 homes across the Republic use this oil as their primary source of heating their homes.

News of the increase comes as householders prepare for the winter, when the need for home heating is at its greatest.

Home heating oil prices rose by 7.2 per cent from August to September alone, the CSO noted.

Rises in heating oil, natural gas and motor fuel costs could wipe out most of what workers will gain through tax cuts and other benefits announced this week in Budget 2026.

Those gains will simply “help people to stand still”, the consumer advocate remarked of the measures announced by Minister for Finance, Simon Harris, on Tuesday.

The US-Iran war, a resulting squeeze on global refining capacity and a weakening in the value of the euro against the dollar, are combining to drive up the price of the kerosene used by Irish people to heat their homes, Cassidy explained.

Motorists also continued to deal with sharp price increases on forecourts, according to CSO.

Fuel excise cuts extended to February as carbon tax is slashed to ease home heating costs

Petrol prices were 14 per cent higher in September than a year earlier, while diesel rose by 22 per cent. This was against a backdrop of a renewal in air strikes by the US on Iran and the absence of a deal that would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and ease trade blockages.

Diesel cost €2.06 a litre on average in the Republic last month while petrol cost €1.96 a litre.

The CSO does not publish national average prices for home heating oil.

“In the month of September we saw significant price movements for fuel and home heating oil,” Anthony Dawson, a statistician in the CSO’s prices division acknowledged.

The CSO’s Consumer Price Index, which measures the cost of living in the Republic, rose 4.1 per cent year-on-year in September, the office confirmed on Thursday.

The most significant increases in the 12 months to September were in housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels, Dawson noted.

Dermot Daly, EY Ireland consumer products and retail lead, said the jump in energy prices in the latest CSO data is “particularly noteworthy”.

“Consumers have shown resilience – household spending is likely to grow 2.5 per cent after inflation this year – but many will have to prioritise essential purchases while taking a more considered approach to discretionary spending,” he said.

“As we move closer to the important Christmas trading period, retailers will be hoping that consumer spending remains resilient despite ongoing cost pressures.

The CSO’s Dawson confirmed that the 4.1 per cent rise in the cost of living was the highest since September 2024, when the increase was also 4.1 per cent.

The Government this week increased the social welfare fuel allowance by €5 to €43 a week in Budget 2026.

It also cut carbon taxes levied on home heating oil to €48.50 a tonne for the current Government’s remaining term in office.

]]>K Neville<![CDATA[Irish Government was warned last year that RTÉ funding was too low]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/regulator-warned-government-last-year-that-rte-funding-was-too-low/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/regulator-warned-government-last-year-that-rte-funding-was-too-low/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 13:36:45 +0000Ireland’s media regulator and an external consultancy firm both told the Government last year that RTÉ’s 2026 budget allocation of €240 million was not adequate to support the broadcaster’s five-year strategy and deliver the reforms the Coalition expected.

The Government was also told the national broadcaster would face “particularly acute” cash flow issues in 2027, even if it received the €260 million earmarked for next year under a 2024 agreement with the previous government.

Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan confirmed on Wednesday that the publicly owned broadcaster will receive €240 million again in 2027, €20 million less than the previous government had guaranteed in 2024.

The decision has ignited a row between Montrose and the Government.

In a report submitted to the minister in July 2025, consultancy firm Oliver & Ohlbaum Associates said that even the €240 million allocated for 2026 “is insufficient to fully support RTÉ’s sustainability, strategy and delivery of public service objectives”.

The report was commissioned by Coimisiún na Meán as part of its annual review of public funding for RTÉ and TG4.

In its letter to the minister accompanying the report, the regulator said it shared the consultants’ view that “the €240 million allocated to RTÉ for 2026 is not fully adequate to support RTÉ’s sustainability, Statement of Strategy and delivery of the [public service media] objects over time”.

The commission said this view aligns with findings of a separate five-year review of funding adequacy for the Republic’s two publicly owned broadcasters, RTÉ and TG4. That review “raised significant concerns regarding RTÉ’s projected cash balance – particularly in 2027″.

Under the terms of the multiyear framework agreed in 2024, most of the broadcaster’s funding is to come from licence fees. RTÉ required a €41.3 million top-up from the exchequer last year and director general Kevin Bakhurst said it would require €54.8 million this year.

On Wednesday, O’Donovan suggested the decision to cut RTÉ’s funding next year relative to the 2024 agreement was due to the slow pace of reform in Montrose.

However, in a letter to Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers, seen by The Irish Times, O’Donovan warned last week that the putative €827 million that was set to be allocated to his department in Budget 2027 was insufficient.

O’Donovan and his junior minister, Charlie McConalogue, said that, among other things, it would mean his department would have to “renege” on the final year of the three-year funding deal for RTÉ.

“In fact, we now envisage a cut to RTÉ funding next year in the order of €11 million,” the ministers told Chambers.

The department received a further €21 million after tense budget negotiations over the weekend, which avoided the €11 million cut. Yet, funding for the broadcaster next year was reduced to €240 million from an expected €260 million.

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[Shares fall as Middle East tanker attacks drive oil prices higher ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/shares-fall-as-middle-east-tanker-attacks-drive-oil-prices-higher/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/shares-fall-as-middle-east-tanker-attacks-drive-oil-prices-higher/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:34:30 +0000Global shares fell on Thursday as oil topped $105 amid fresh tanker attacks by Iran, which threaten to curtail a recent uptick in flows from the Middle East and adding to worries over rising inflation globally.

Rival Micron Technology was down 1.8 per cent.

Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Broadcom is lining up $50 ‌billion ‌in ​financing for OpenAI, with Oracle also seeking an unspecified sum, spurring fears that large debt issuance by technology companies could intensify the competition for capital.

Broadcom and Oracle were down 1.4 per cent and 2.1 per cent, respectively, amid wider weakness in ⁠tech stocks. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg, Reuters

Clary<![CDATA[Top Goldman Sachs executives to get $500m in one of largest such payouts in Wall Street history]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/goldman-sachs-to-pay-top-executives-500mn-in-special-bonuses/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/goldman-sachs-to-pay-top-executives-500mn-in-special-bonuses/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:09:34 +0000Goldman Sachs’ most senior executives are in line to receive more than $500 million (€446.2 million) in special bonuses from a five-year incentive plan, one of the biggest payouts of its kind in the Wall Street bank’s history.

The lender is preparing to hand out equity awards to a group of its most senior leaders that would exceed $500 million at Goldman’s current share price, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The payout is part of a long-term incentive scheme the bank disclosed in 2021, with the final value of the bonus pool determined by the bank’s stock market performance relative to peers at the end of October, meaning it could still change, another person said.

The bumper package, first reported by Bloomberg, comes after Goldman’s share price outperformed most of its Wall Street rivals over the past five years.

The special incentive scheme was agreed at a time when Wall Street banks were benefiting from record dealmaking and a boom in “blank cheque” companies as the industry rebounded from the Covid pandemic.

Goldman Sachs reports best quarter in five years even as fixed-income traders disappoint

Goldman chief executive David Solomon is expected to receive the largest chunk of the bonus pool, taking home about $100 million in share-based awards.

John Waldron, Goldman’s second-in-command who is widely seen as the heir apparent to Solomon, is also among the beneficiaries of the scheme, as well as other members of Goldman’s management committee from 2021 who are still with the bank.

The performance-based stock for Solomon was worth about $30 million when Goldman announced the plan in 2021, while Waldron’s was worth about $20 million.

Solomon and Waldron, who is Goldman’s president and chief operating officer, have led the investment bank since 2018. The pair were also both granted five-year retention bonuses, worth $80 million apiece, at the start of 2025.

Goldman paid Solomon $47 million last year, an increase of more than one-fifth from the previous year and his highest remuneration since he took the helm at the Wall Street bank.

The first half of his tenure was marred by a lossmaking expansion into retail banking, which was at odds with the investment bank’s Wall Street pedigree and prompted fierce criticism of Solomon’s leadership.

After billions of dollars in losses, Goldman largely exited the consumer push and has since doubled down on investment banking, trading and money management. The bank’s shares are up about 180 per cent over the past three years.

Goldman said: “The board created these awards to achieve three principal objectives: align compensation with rigorous performance thresholds, ensure leadership continuity and enhance retention of our top talent in an increasingly competitive market.” - Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

Fallon<![CDATA[Bar manager let go after miscarriage awarded €25,000 ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/08/bar-manager-let-go-after-miscarriage-awarded-25000/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/08/bar-manager-let-go-after-miscarriage-awarded-25000/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:05:54 +0000A Galway hospitality firm which dismissed a manager just 11 days after she suffered a miscarriage, before trying to claim that maternity protection law didn’t apply since she wasn’t pregnant any longer, has been ordered to pay her €25,000.

Fadeside Ltd, a subsidiary of the Connacht Hospitality Group, has been ordered by the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) to compensate a former manager at its Residence Hotel and 1520 Bar in Galway City for terminating her employment in October 2023 on the stated basis of underperformance.

It is said to be the first time a worker has sought to have the minimum service requirements of the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977 set aside under maternity protection law in the circumstances of a miscarriage.

Normally, an employee requires 12 months’ service before they can pursue a complaint for unfair dismissal – a limitation disapplied in relation to pregnant workers, who are shielded from day one.

The complainant fell ill and was admitted to A&E in September 2023. She found out then that she had been pregnant and was having a miscarriage, she said in evidence to the tribunal.

At the time, she was just under 11 months into a new €60,000-a-year job as general manager at the hotel and bar in Galway’s Latin Quarter.

She said that, after phoning in sick, group HR manager Jackie O’Dowd reached her by phone and said the miscarriage “would make [the complainant] want to have a baby even more”.

At the WRC, O’Dowd denied making the remark.

The complainant said she told O’Dowd in reply that getting pregnant was not something she had planned.

Having returned to work in the first week of October 2023, the worker met her line manager, Wayne Neilon, later telling the WRC she wanted to discuss her working hours and other business maters, she said.

The complainant said Neilon told her she “did not have the core competencies” for the job.

O’Dowd then arrived and asked whether the complainant wanted to resign, remarking that perhaps she “needed a break” because of the miscarriage, the complainant said.

She was told at the meeting that her probation would not be extended and received a letter of dismissal citing “work performance” the following day, the tribunal was told.

The complainant said Neilon had told her months earlier, in May 2023, that she had passed her probation, and that she said so at the October meeting.

In any case, the WRC noted the complainant’s contract capped the maximum probation period at 11 months; by the time of the October meeting, she had 11 months and two days’ service.

The firm’s solicitor, Pat Mullins of O’Flynn Exhams LLP, failed in March of last year in an attempt to have the case thrown out, arguing that enhanced workplace protections under the Maternity Protection Act did not extend to the complainant.

“At the time of the dismissal, the complainant was not, in fact, pregnant, and I say it is a substantial stretch of the interpretation of that part of the Act to state that it includes a previous miscarriage,” Mullins said.

Counsel for the worker, Ian FitzHarris, with Orlaith J Byrne & Co solicitors, said the sacking was just 11 days after the pregnancy loss, his client having worked just five more days after her absence, he said.

“Five days and then they sacked her. The phrase in the legislation is ‘pregnancy-related matters’,” counsel said.

Adjudicator Louise Boyle rejected the respondent’s stance on maternity rights. “It is not in dispute that a miscarriage arises from pregnancy,” she wrote.

“I find that in all the circumstances it lacks credibility that the complainant’s employment was terminated for poor performance,” she wrote.

She concluded the respondent had failed to demonstrate there were the “exceptional circumstances” required to dismiss a worker entitled to maternity protections and awarded €25,000 for unfair dismissal.

]]>urbazon<![CDATA[Tesco to open four new Irish stores as expansion continues]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/sales-in-tescos-irish-business-rise/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/sales-in-tescos-irish-business-rise/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 06:44:08 +0000

Tesco plans to open four new Irish stores, including large supermarkets and further Express outlets, in the coming months.

Interim results published on Wednesday by the British grocer showed it has plans to add a further 60,000 sq ft of Irish retail space before February next year.

A spokeswoman for Tesco, which opened nine new Irish stores in the past 12 in months, told The Irish Times that the expansion would include two new superstores in Donegal Town and Clongriffin in Dublin.

She added that new Express stores will also be opened in Montpelier in Dublin and Ballincollig in Cork.

The company’s latest results showed sales at Tesco’s Irish business rose in the first half of the year, driven by growth in its fresh and packaged food offering.

Tesco, which claims a 24.1 per cent share of the Irish grocery market, said strong like-for-like sales growth of 4.1 per cent was driven by volume increases. Total sales growth of 6.7 per cent was driven by a contribution from new space.

Like-for-like sales in its food business grew 4.4 per cent compared with the same period in 2025, with the company’s Tesco Finest sales rising almost 13 per cent year on year.

The company’s online business also surged, growing by close to 12 per cent, lifted by the wider roll-out of its Whoosh same-day delivery service to more stores in the second half of 2025.

Non-food sales were up 1.5 per cent on a like-for-like basis.

The wider Tesco group lifted the bottom end of ‌its full-year profit outlook on Thursday after reporting a 6.5 per cent increase for its ​first half, even as a very hot summer weighed on sales volumes across the industry.

The group said it made an adjusted operating profit ⁠of £1.78 billion for the 26 weeks to August ‌29th, ‌on ​sales, excluding VAT sales tax and fuel, up 2 per cent to £33.8 billion.

UK like-for-like sales ⁠for the half ​rose 1.5 per cent, having been up ​1.8 per cent in the first quarter.

Monthly industry data has ‌shown Tesco lost a little ​market share in the second quarter. However, it was ⁠up against a tough comparative ⁠performance ​in the same quarter last year when UK like-for-like sales rose 4.6 per cent, helped by disruption at competitors Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Asda.

The conflict in the Middle East, and its impact on energy prices, also created uncertainty for many ‌households during the first ⁠half.

Tesco, whose shares have risen 8 per cent so far this year, is now forecasting adjusted operating ‌profit of £3.15 billion to £3.3 billion for its year to end-February ​2027, versus previous guidance of £3 billion to £3.3 ​billion and the £3.152 billion made in 2025/26. – Additional reporting: Reuters

]]><![CDATA[Price of Porsche’s top models to rise by 20% to more than €330,000 by 2030]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/porsche-to-raise-top-model-prices-by-20/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/porsche-to-raise-top-model-prices-by-20/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 13:39:57 +0000Porsche will raise the average price of its most expensive models by about a fifth by 2030, as the German sports-car maker aims to echo Ferrari’s strategy of using exclusivity to boost profits.

Chief executive Michael Leiters outlined a years-long plan at an investor day on Wednesday to revive Porsche’s fortunes by selling fewer but more upmarket cars following a costly unwinding of its electric vehicle ambitions last year.

“We want to further elevate our positioning, protect the exclusivity of Porsche and gain pricing power,” said Leiters, the former McLaren boss who took over in January. “This brand has a lot of power.”

The average price of Porsche’s top models will increase to more than €330,000 by the end of the decade from about €270,000 this year, while the proportion of its portfolio made up of top-end models is expected to rise to 45 per cent from a third currently.

Porsche’s shift towards higher-margin sports cars and limited editions of exclusive models echoes a signature Ferrari strategy that has helped the Italian carmaker achieve an industry-beating operating profit margin of 30 per cent.

Porsche historically contributed outsize profits to the Volkswagen Group thanks to explosive growth in China. But its fortunes have reversed dramatically as sales plummeted in the world’s largest car market and it was hit by higher US tariffs. The company has also taken huge writedowns to reinvest in petrol models it abandoned during a big pivot to electric cars.

Leiters’ strategy will result in a much smaller Porsche, with the company reducing the number of vehicles it needs to sell to turn a profit to fewer than 200,000 units. The group delivered about 320,000 cars in 2023, when it had an operating profit margin of 18 per cent, but last year its margin plunged to 1.1 per cent on deliveries of roughly 280,000 cars.

The group on Wednesday maintained its target to achieve an operating profit margin of 10 to 15 per cent and an automotive net cash flow margin of up to 12 per cent by 2030. It will target a profit margin of 15 per cent by 2035.

Porsche is betting on a new combustion-engine version of its bestselling Macan, due in 2028, to revive its profits and offset falling sales in China.

It also plans to unveil a new SUV, which will come in petrol and plug-in hybrid versions, in the same year and develop a new super-sports car to be priced higher than its signature 911 model.

“We are becoming more selective about where we can compete and more ambitious in the segments where we see the strongest fit with our brand,” Leiters said.

Leiters, who previously served as Ferrari’s chief technology officer, said its plan to shift sales towards more expensive, higher-margin products would be accompanied by 20 per cent cuts in product development costs and the number of model variants it makes.

The company has already reached a deal with unions to cut 9,000 jobs – or roughly 20 per cent of its workforce – by 2035.

UBS analyst Patrick Hummel said Porsche should “comfortably” return to double-digit profit margins by the end of the decade if Leiters was successful in executing his strategy.

“It’s replicating what Ferrari has been successful at. Porsche also has the potential to [sell] more at the upper end and offer more exclusivity with the right models,” he said.

Leiters told the FT last week that “there won’t be a 911 electric”, although the company is going ahead with the electric version of its 718 sports car next year.

On Wednesday, Porsche said it would aim for a two-to-one split between petrol and plug-in hybrids versus EVs.

Scott Sherwood, an independent analyst of luxury car brands, said Ferrari had been able to build its strategy around “scarcity” because it only sold about 14,000 models a year. Even with the right sizing, Porsche’s scale would be much bigger, he said.

“They have a big brand challenge. Porsche is a sports car brand, and sports cars at supercar pricing only works with a small group of brands with the most hard-core loyalists,” Sherwood said. “It’s a bit like Rolex deciding they want to go after Patek Philippe buyers.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Mike Kemp<![CDATA[EasyJet to cut 700,000 seats from winter flight schedule amid rising fuel costs]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/transport/2026/10/08/easyjet-doubles-winter-flight-cuts-amid-rising-costs/https://www.irishtimes.com/transport/2026/10/08/easyjet-doubles-winter-flight-cuts-amid-rising-costs/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 14:59:25 +0000EasyJet will cut another 700,000 seats from its winter flight schedule to save on fuel as the low-cost airline steps up efforts to curb costs during the industry’s lean season.

Chief executive Kenton Jarvis said the company was scaling back capacity over the quieter months to prevent it paying higher sums for fuel, which has rocketed in price since the Iran conflict in February.

Earlier in the summer, Easyjet cut about 700,000 seats from its winter flights. Jarvis said the airline would now remove between 600,000 and 700,000 more – the equivalent of about two days’ worth of flying.

The budget carrier, one of Europe’s biggest airlines, typically offers about 50 million seats on flights over the winter season, which runs from October to end of March.

“People are taking capacity out, we see that across all competitors,” he told the FT, adding that was “no surprise” given fuel costs. “I honestly think it’s been quite a surprise for the industry that fuel has stayed as high as it is.”
